description: core §4.2 (0.26; the open cases decided in 0.27), a late joiner's merge. A stamp is `{time, id}`: `time` an NTP64 value (unit 2^-32 s), `id` the 128-bit id of the HLC that issued it, written as zenoh writes an id and a zid: lowercase hexadecimal without leading zeros. `order`: two stamps → `expect`, `less`, `equal` or `greater` for `a` against `b`. Stamps compare by time; on equal times by id, as zenoh's `Timestamp` compares them: the id's 128-bit value written as 16 bytes little-endian (least significant byte first), the two byte strings compared lexicographically from the first byte. So the least significant byte that differs decides, which is not the ids' order as integers. `cases`: one key's arrivals, in arrival order, whichever path brought each (S4's GET or the subscription), each a `stamp` or `null` (unstamped) and a `kind` (`put` or `delete`; a `reply_del` is a `delete` with its stamp) → `expect.kept`, whether each arrival replaces what the key holds. A stamped arrival is kept when the key holds nothing, only unstamped arrivals, or a lower stamp; an equal stamp is the same mutation, not kept again; a higher one held makes it stale. An unstamped arrival is kept when the key holds nothing or only unstamped arrivals (the later replacing the earlier), and never when it holds a stamped one. The kind never decides. Across two ids this is a tool's merge, kept for as long as it follows (observer §4.1); a consumer orders across two ids by core §4.3's consumer rule instead, keeping a value under an id other than its held value's (`scenarios/state.md` §7).

order.note: equal times: 100's low byte 00 is below 2's 02, though 0x100 is above 0x2
equal times: the low bytes ff and fe decide, not the high bytes 1 and 2
equal times: a 16-byte id whose low byte is 00 is below 1
equal times, equal low bytes: the next byte decides
